1:
With Josiah newly fallen at Megiddo, the throne passes to his son, and the witnesses read the accession as the first step of a swift descent. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the pace of the whole chapter: as the kingdom of Judah advanced with rapid steps toward its destruction by the Chaldeans, so the Chronicler hurries over the four kings who reigned between Josiah's death and the fall of Jerusalem, giving of each little more than his age at accession, a brief characterization of his conduct toward God, and the events that step by step brought on the ruin. The people of the land raised Jehoahaz, then twenty-three years old, but he had been king only three months when Necho of Egypt deposed him, fined the land a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold, and set his brother Eliakim on the throne — the sequence Keil draws from the fuller record at 2 Kings 23:30-35.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the moment of the seizure: after Necho had discomfited Josiah he pressed straight on toward Carchemish, and in the interval, Josiah dying of his wounds, the people made his son king — an act taken without the conqueror's leave that Necho would soon undo. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the bare notice into a meditation on God's patience. The destruction of Judah and Jerusalem comes on here by degrees, and Henry reads the slowness itself as mercy: God so ordered it to show that he has no pleasure in the ruin of sinners, but had rather they would turn and live, and therefore gives them both time and inducement to repent, waiting to be gracious. Of Jehoahaz himself he is severe and brief — set up by the people, in one quarter of a year deposed by Pharaoh-Necho and carried prisoner to Egypt, the land fined for setting him up; and of this young prince we hear no more. Had he trodden in the steps of his father's piety he might have reigned long and prospered; but because, as Kings records, he did evil in the sight of the LORD, his triumphing was short and his joy but for a moment.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds the genealogical note that Jehoahaz, also called Shallum, was not the firstborn, as 1 Chron. 3:15 shows, so that the people's choice reached past an elder brother; the verse agrees, he says, with the account at 2 Kings 23:30. The witnesses do not divide. Together they frame the chapter as a swift, sorrowful chronicle of a doomed throne, in which even the people's hasty crowning of a son of Josiah cannot arrest the judgment already gathering over the house of David.
2:
The reign is measured in a single breath — twenty-three years old, three months upon the throne — and the witnesses dwell on the extraordinary brevity and on what the Chronicler chooses to leave unsaid. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch return to the historian's method: of each of these last kings he records little more than the age at accession and a short verdict on his walk before God, before pressing on to the events that hastened the collapse. So condensed is the account that Jehoahaz is given no space to act at all; three months was time enough for Necho to intervene, but not for the young king to leave any mark of his own upon the kingdom. The very compression is a kind of commentary: a reign so brief that it can be told without a single deed of its own is a reign the historian is content to hurry past, that he may reach the greater ruin toward which the whole book is bending.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the notice beside its parallel and marks a small omission. The figure of twenty-three agrees with 2 Kings 23:31, except that Kings, as is its custom, adds the name of the queen-mother — Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah — which the Chronicler here drops, though the Septuagint supplies it. It is a characteristic trace of the compiler's haste: even the domestic detail that the book of Kings preserves is pared away in this flying record of a reign that scarcely began.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry notices a graver silence. Where 2 Kings 23:32 pronounces Jehoahaz evil in the sight of the LORD, the Chronicler passes the verdict by, so that the moral judgment on the king must be sought in the elder history; yet the brevity of the reign is itself a kind of sentence. Henry had drawn the lesson already: this young prince, had he walked in his father's piety, might have reigned long, but doing evil, his joy was but for a moment. The three-month reign preaches the same truth the whole chapter will unfold — that a crown quickly given is quickly taken when the man who wears it forsakes the God of his fathers, and that the throne of David, once the surest seat in the world, has become in these closing days the most precarious. The witnesses agree in reading the terse obituary not as neglect but as proportion: a king who did nothing worthy of memory receives a memorial of a single line, while the swiftness of his fall speaks louder than any recorded deed.
3:
Necho's undoing of the people's choice draws the witnesses to the manner and the meaning of the deposition. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as an act of naked supremacy: the king of Egypt now considered Judah conquered and tributary to him, and because the people had set up Jehoahaz without his consent, he dethroned him and put his brother in his place, perhaps for no other reason than to display his overlordship. He directs the reader to the fuller notes at 2 Kings 23:31-35 for the particulars the Chronicler compresses.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the verb. The king of Egypt did not merely “put him down” but “removed him,” the sense the Greek of Third Esdras makes explicit by adding “from reigning,” a phrase the context almost demands. On the place of the deed the versions diverge: the Septuagint, following 2 Kings 23:33, has Necho bind him at Riblah in the land of Hamath so that he should not reign in Jerusalem, while the Syriac and the Vulgate support the existing Hebrew text. Ellicott locates Riblah in Syria upon the Orontes and suggests that Necho may have ordered or enticed Jehoahaz to meet him there, where the young king was seized — a detail that fits the northward march toward Carchemish the campaign was pursuing.

On the fine laid upon the kingdom the witnesses converge. The clause that the English renders “condemned the land” Ellicott gives more plainly as “fined the land,” matching the idiom of Kings, “laid a fine upon the land”; the sum was a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold. The weight of that exaction is not lost on the reader who recalls, with the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, that the land was fined for setting up Jehoahaz: the people who had crowned a son of Josiah in defiance of Egypt now paid for their presumption, and the impost fell on the whole nation rather than on the deposed king alone. So the verse gathers the chapter's early theme. A conqueror's word can lift a king onto the throne and cast him down again at will, and the independence Judah had enjoyed under Josiah is already gone; the people's choice counts for nothing against Pharaoh's, and the treasury that should have served the temple begins, instead, to drain away into the mouth of a foreign master. The deposition of Jehoahaz is thus more than a change of rulers; it is the first tribute of a kingdom that has ceased, in all but name, to be its own.
4:
The installation of a puppet king lays bare how completely Judah's sovereignty has passed into a stranger's hand, and the witnesses attend to the naming as much as to the crowning. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the verse agrees with 2 Kings 23:34, where Necho makes Eliakim king and turns his name to Jehoiakim. The changing of the name is itself an act of dominion: to rename a king is to own him, and the Egyptian marks his vassal by fixing a new name upon him. Of Jehoahaz, carried off, Ellicott observes that the Chronicler's “carried him to Egypt” is more exactly “made him come,” while Kings adds the mournful note that “he came to Egypt, and died there,” the fulfilment of Jeremiah's lament over the king who should go away and return no more, at Jer. 22:10-12. The Septuagint, he adds, expands the verse with a picture of the taxation that followed, each man of the land assessed according to his ability to render the silver and the gold into the mouth of Pharaoh-Necho.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the sequence within their compressed account of the reign: Necho made Eliakim his brother king over Judah and Jerusalem, turned his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz to Egypt. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the humiliation the plain words carry. Jehoiakim was set up by the king of Egypt, an old enemy to their land, who now gave what king he pleased to the kingdom and what name he pleased to the king; he made Eliakim king and called him Jehoiakim in token of his authority over him. The very honour of a crown, Henry sees, has become a badge of servitude, conferred and labelled by a heathen conqueror.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke folds the episode into his survey of the whole chapter, marking Jehoiakim as one who would reign wickedly eleven years before he too was dethroned and led toward Babylon. The witnesses do not contend; together they read the verse as the deepening of the shame begun in the deposition. One brother is dragged to die in Egypt while another is seated on the throne and rechristened at a Pharaoh's pleasure; the house of David, so lately independent under Josiah, now holds its crown at the sufferance of a foreign king, and even the names of its rulers are no longer their own. The stage is set for the ruin that the abominations of this renamed king will hasten.
5:
The formal accession of Jehoiakim — twenty-five years old, eleven years upon the throne, doing evil in the sight of the LORD his God — draws the witnesses chiefly into history and philology, and into a sharp exchange with a modern critic. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott anchors the figures to 2 Kings 23:36, where the mother's name is again supplied, and notes that the verdict of 2 Kings 23:37 adds “according to all that his fathers had done.” He pauses over the new power now rising on the horizon: Nebuchadnezzar, whose name he renders “Nebo, guard the crown,” son of Nabopolassar, who had founded the dynasty by a successful revolt against Assyria. His inscriptions, Ellicott observes, concern chiefly the building of palaces and temples rather than campaigns — a brick in the Zürich Museum names him “restorer of Esagila and Ezida” — and no truly historical inscription survives save a fragment on his Egyptian campaign and an illegible one on the rocks of the Nahr-el-Kelb near Beirut.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the plain data — Jehoiakim at his accession twenty-five, reigning eleven years, evil in the eyes of Jahve his God — and set his reign against the record of 2 Kings 23:36 and following. The deeper dispute, which Ellicott presses, concerns whether Jehoiakim was actually deported. Nebuchadnezzar, having defeated Necho at Carchemish in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, as Jer. 46:2 records, appears to have left the king of Judah to reign as a vassal after a severe humiliation. Against this, Thenius (as reported by Ellicott) argued that the chronicler deliberately represented Jehoiakim as carried alive to Babylon in his last year, in order to leave ample scope for the fulfilment of Jeremiah's prophecy. Ellicott rejects the charge as resting not on historical grounds but on a subjective prejudice against the chronicler.

A subordinate tangle concerns the date. Ellicott notes that Daniel 1:1, by a transcriber's error, places this first capture of Jerusalem in the third year of Jehoiakim, whereas Nebuchadnezzar became king only in the fourth. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, gathering the strands, marks Jehoiakim as the king who cast the fear of God behind him and hastened the nation toward captivity. The witnesses stand together where it matters: the reign that opens with a stock verdict of “evil” is the reign under which the Babylonian shadow first falls across Judah, and the critical quibbles about deportation and dates cannot soften the judgment the sacred writer means to record.
6:
The coming of Nebuchadnezzar and the binding of Jehoiakim in fetters fix for the witnesses the very hour at which the long Chaldean servitude begins. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the clause with care — “bound him with brazen double fetters to carry him to Babylon” — and identify this as Nebuchadnezzar's first campaign against Judah, spoken of also in 2 Kings 24 and Daniel 1:1-2. The capture of Jerusalem at which the king was fettered fell, they reckon from Jer. 46:2 and the parallel notices, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, about 606 B.C.; and with it the seventy years of the Chaldean servitude of Judah commence — the count that the last verses of the chapter will bring to its close.

Keil and Delitzsch are firm that the intention to deport was not carried through: Nebuchadnezzar did not remove Jehoiakim to Babylon but allowed him to reign on at Jerusalem as his servant and vassal. To turn the infinitive “to carry him” into a completed act, or to supply the words “and he carried him away,” they judge quite arbitrary; the Chronicler records the purpose, not its execution, and the reader is not to press the phrase beyond what it says. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same reticence: the king of Babylon came up against Jehoiakim, seized and bound him with a design to carry him to Babylon, but it seems he either changed his mind and suffered him to reign as his vassal, or death released the prisoner before he was carried away.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supplies the chronological refinement that will matter for the seventy years. Referring the reader to 2 Kings 24:1, he cites Archbishop Ussher's view that Jehoiakim remained three years after this subjection a tributary to the Chaldeans, and that it is from this period that the seventy years' captivity predicted by Jeremiah is to be reckoned. The witnesses do not divide. Whether one dates the servitude from the first fettering or from the settled vassalage that followed, they agree that this campaign is the decisive turn: the Egyptian master who had renamed Judah's king is gone, a greater power has come up from the east, and the clock of the exile has begun to run. What looks in the verse like a change of overlords is in truth the opening of the long night the prophets had foretold.
7:
The carrying of the temple vessels into a Babylonian shrine is, for the witnesses, both a plain fact of plunder and a pointed act of judgment. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record simply that Nebuchadnezzar carried off vessels of the house of the LORD to Babylon and put them in his temple there, a spoliation that Kings does not mention but which, as the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds, is confirmed by Daniel 1:2. Ellicott identifies the sanctuary that received them as the temple of Merodach, or Bel, the god whom Nebuchadnezzar's inscriptions so constantly invoke — the great temple of Bel-Merodach that was reckoned by Herodotus among the wonders of the world.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the moral symmetry of the exchange. No temple in the world, he supposes, was so richly furnished as that of Jerusalem; and the sin of Judah had been to bring the idols of the heathen into God's temple. Now their punishment answers their crime: the vessels of the LORD's house are carried away to the service of the gods of the nations. If men will profane God's institutions by their sins, Henry reflects, it is just with God to suffer them to be profaned by their enemies. The very holiness the people had defiled is now handed over to be defiled by pagans, so that the plunder is not mere loss but retribution measured to the offence.

Henry traces the vessels further through the prophetic word. These were the vessels about whose return the false prophets had flattered the people with vain hopes, which Jeremiah answered at Jer. 27:16 by declaring that the rest should follow them to Babylon, and so they did, as Jer. 27:21-22 foretold. And as the carrying away of these vessels began the calamity of Jerusalem, so their profanation would one day fill the measure of Babylon's own iniquity; for when Belshazzar drank wine from them to the honour of his gods, the handwriting on the wall pronounced his doom, as Dan. 5:3 and the verses that follow relate. The witnesses do not divide. They read the removal of the vessels as the first installment of the exile and as a lesson written in sacred gold: what is stolen from God to serve idols is repaid by God into the hands of idolaters, until at the appointed hour the profaners are themselves judged, and the vessels, having witnessed against Jerusalem, witness at last against Babylon.
8:
The closing formula for Jehoiakim — the rest of his acts, his abominations, and “that which was found in him” — sets the witnesses to weighing the king's hidden guilt and the record that half conceals it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott glosses “his abominations” as his crimes against God and man, most likely acts of idolatry and tyranny, and points to the indictments of the prophet — the covetousness, the shedding of innocent blood, the building of a great house by unrighteousness charged at Jer. 22:13-19. The phrase “that which was found in him” he takes, as at 2 Chron. 19:3, of the king's general character and conduct; and he observes that, as with Amon at 2 Chron. 33:25, the last particulars of the reign are omitted in this rapid notice, which was memorable chiefly for Nebuchadnezzar's invasion.

Ellicott records a textual quarrel here too. The Septuagint substitutes the account of 2 Kings 24:5-6, interpolating the notice that Jehoiakim was “buried with his fathers in the garden of Uzza.” Thenius (as reported by Ellicott) asserted that these words certainly stood in the original text but were suppressed by the chronicler and the editor of Kings because they conflict with Jeremiah's prophecy that Jehoiakim should have the burial of an ass and be cast out beyond the gates, at Jer. 22:18-19. Ellicott plainly regards that very conflict as the reason Thenius is so confident of their genuineness, and lets the suspicion answer itself.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads “that which was found in him” more narrowly, of the crime of rebellion against the king of Babylon, which for a time Jehoiakim kept close in his own breast and afterward, when he saw fit, disclosed, and so was convicted of it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry allows both senses — the treachery found in him toward the king of Babylon, or, as some Jewish writers understood it, certain private marks or idolatrous signatures found upon his dead body, such cuttings in the flesh as God had forbidden at Lev. 19:28. The witnesses do not finally divide. Whether the thing found in him was perjured rebellion or secret idolatry, they agree that the formula which seems merely to defer to the royal annals in fact hides a hardened and abominable reign, and that the Chronicler's reticence is not praise but a drawing of the veil over a king whose evil hastened his people's ruin.
9:
The brief reign of Jehoiachin — three months and ten days, ended by deportation — is nearly swallowed by a single textual crux, and the witnesses gather almost entirely around the king's age. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that Chronicles gives his age at accession as eight years, while 2 Kings 24:8 reads eighteen; the Septuagint and Vulgate follow the eight, but several Hebrew codices, the Syriac and Arabic, and many manuscripts of the Greek read eighteen here as well. The number eight, they judge, is clearly an orthographic error — a verdict, they add, that even Thenius acknowledges — though Bertheau (as reported by Keil) defends the eight of the text as original and treats the eighteen of Kings as the corruption.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott decides the matter on both textual and moral grounds. The difference turns on the omission of the smallest Hebrew letter, the yod, which as a numeral stands for ten; and, more tellingly, what the prophet Ezekiel says of Jehoiachin could not apply to a boy of eight, for according to Ezek. 19:5-9 he “devoured men, and forced widows, and wasted cities.” Ellicott therefore reads eighteen as the true figure. On the odd precision “three months and ten days,” where Kings has only “three months,” he reports the suggestion of Thenius that the ten days were added so that the catastrophe of the reign might fall on a tenth day of the month, matching the investment and fall of the city under Zedekiah — a conjecture Ellicott passes on without endorsing.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke simply refers the reader to his notes on 2 Kings 24:6-15, while the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the human sense of the number. Jehoiachin, called also Jeconiah, reigned long enough to show his evil inclination, and after three months and ten days the king of Babylon fetched him away captive with more of the goodly vessels of the temple; the eight years, Henry allows, seems a mistake of the transcriber for eighteen, unless one supposes that his father took him at eight years old to share in the government. The witnesses do not divide on what matters. However the numeral is resolved, they agree that this was a full-grown and evil man, not an innocent child; that his reign of a hundred days was but time enough to earn the verdict “he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD”; and that his swift removal to Babylon is one more step in the measured descent of the house of David toward the exile.
10:
The turn of the year brings Jehoiachin's deportation and the raising up of the last king of Judah, and the witnesses attend both to the timing and to the strange word “brother.” The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott explains that “when the year was expired” means, as the margin shows, “at the return of the year” — the spring, the season when kings went forth to war, as at 2 Sam. 11:1 and 1 Kings 20:22. Kings gives the full account of the siege and surrender of Jerusalem and the deportation of the king with his princes and men of war; the Chronicler notes only that Nebuchadnezzar brought Jehoiachin to Babylon with the goodly vessels of the house of the LORD, some of which, as v.7 had shown, were already gone.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the notice into the reign it introduces: Nebuchadnezzar made Zedekiah king over Judah and Jerusalem, a king of twenty-one years who would reign eleven and fill up the measure of the nation's sins, so that the LORD was at last compelled to give the kingdom up to destruction. On the word “brother” the witnesses correct the text with one voice. Ellicott points out that Zedekiah was in fact the uncle of Jehoiachin, a son of Josiah and brother of Jehoiakim, so that “brother” must here mean “kinsman,” as often; the versions read “his father's brother,” which he takes for a correction, and Thenius supposed the word for “uncle” had become illegible in the manuscript the chronicler used. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees exactly: Zedekiah is “largely so called” his brother, being really his uncle, the son of Josiah.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke adds the detail of the renaming that the verse omits: the new king's name was at first Mattaniah, and the king of Babylon changed it to Zedekiah, as 2 Kings 24:17 records. The witnesses do not divide, and the pattern they trace is grim in its repetition. As Necho had renamed Eliakim, so now Nebuchadnezzar renames Mattaniah; twice within a few years a foreign conqueror sets a son or brother of Josiah on the throne and stamps him with a name of his own choosing. The crown of David has become a thing bestowed at an emperor's pleasure and labelled at his whim, and the man now seated under it — uncle to the boy just carried off — will prove the last to wear it.
11:
The accession of Zedekiah opens the final act, and the witnesses read the twenty-one-year-old king's eleven-year reign as the filling up of a measure long in the pouring. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the scene against the deepest of ironies: Abraham, God's friend, had been called out of that very country, from Ur of the Chaldees, when God took him into covenant, as Gen. 11:31 tells; and now his degenerate seed are carried into that country again, to signify that they had forfeited all the kindness with which they had been regarded for the father's sake, and the benefit of the covenant into which he was called — all now undone again. Zedekiah, Henry judges, brought the ruin upon himself by his folly, conducting himself ill toward both God and the king of Babylon; had he but made God his friend, or been true to his covenant with Nebuchadnezzar, the ruin might have been stayed.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the plain data against 2 Kings 24:18, which adds the mother's name, Hamutal — the same who had borne Jehoahaz, so that the first and last of Josiah's reigning sons were full brothers by one mother. The clause about Jeremiah and the mouth of the LORD, he notes, is not in Kings; and he marks out the two special sins that this and the following verse will lay to Zedekiah's charge — his disregard of the prophet's counsel and his perjury toward Nebuchadnezzar. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch name the same pair: Zedekiah brought the kingdom to destruction by not humbling himself before Jeremiah speaking from the mouth of Jahve, and by rebelling against the king who had made him swear by God, hardening his neck and his heart so that he did not return to the LORD the God of Israel.

Henry presses the lesson of that first sin with a preacher's edge. It was expected that this mighty prince, high as he was, should humble himself before a poor prophet when Jeremiah spoke from the mouth of the LORD — should submit to his admonitions and lay himself under the commanding power of the word of God in his mouth; and because he would not make himself a servant to God, he was made a slave to his enemies. God will find some way to humble those who will not humble themselves. The witnesses do not divide. They read the opening verse of the last reign as the hinge of the whole tragedy: a king young enough to have turned, warned by a living prophet, bound by a sworn oath, who chose stiffness of neck over repentance, and so drew down upon Jerusalem the doom the following verses will describe.
12:
The charge that Zedekiah “humbled not himself before Jeremiah the prophet” becomes for the witnesses the moral center of the king's ruin. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch place it first among his two great sins: he did evil in the sight of the LORD his God and would not humble himself before the prophet who spoke from the mouth of Jahve, a refusal that runs on into the rebellion and the stiffened neck of the next verse. The failure is not ignorance but pride; the word of God came to him plainly and repeatedly by Jeremiah, and the king would not bend beneath it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, who had made this the first count against Zedekiah, dwells on the strangeness of the demand and the justice of the outcome. It was expected that so mighty a prince should humble himself before a poor prophet when Jeremiah spoke in the name of the LORD, submitting to his admonitions and being ruled by his counsels; and because the king would not thus make himself a servant to God, he was made a slave to his enemies. Jeremiah, mean as his figure was, had been set over the nations and kingdoms, as Jer. 1:10 declared, and whoever would not humble themselves before him found it was at their peril. God will find some way, Henry insists, to humble those who will not humble themselves.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns from the single king to the whole dynasty with a kind of exasperated grief. Was there ever, he asks, such a set of weak and infatuated men as the Jewish kings? They had the fullest evidence that they were only deputies to God Almighty, and could not expect to retain the throne any longer than they were faithful to their Lord; and yet with all this conviction they lived wickedly and labored to set up idolatry in the place of the worship of their Maker. After bearing with them long, the divine mercy at last gave them up, their case being now utterly hopeless: they sinned, Clarke says, till there was no remedy. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Zedekiah's evil was not chiefly a matter of gross crime but of a fatal refusal — the refusal of a warned and privileged king to bow before the living word of God — and that this hardness, repeated through a whole line of kings, is what finally exhausted the patience of heaven and sealed the sentence upon Jerusalem.
13:
Zedekiah's rebellion against the king who had put him under oath, and the stiffening of his neck against the LORD, draw the witnesses to the aggravation of perjury and the anatomy of a hardened heart. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott explains that when Nebuchadnezzar appointed Zedekiah his vassal-king he would naturally have made him swear fealty by the God of his fathers. The fact is not specially recorded in Kings, yet the prophet Ezekiel makes it the very point of a prophecy against the king and his grandees at Ezek. 17:11-21, where the LORD speaks of “mine oath that he hath despised.” To break faith with a heathen overlord was to profane the name of God by whom the oath was sworn, and so the political treachery was at bottom a sin against heaven.

Ellicott traces the language of hardening — “stiffened his neck and hardened his heart” — through its kindred expressions at Deut. 2:30, 2 Kings 17:14, and Jer. 19:15. He is careful, though, to draw the king's portrait justly: Zedekiah was not personally unfavorable to Jeremiah, and consulted him more than once, but he was too weak and too timorous to stand by the prophet's counsel in defiance of the princes who were intriguing with Egypt. The tragedy is of a soft man who hardens himself, ruled by the courtiers he feared rather than by the God he half believed.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley sharpens the guilt of the broken oath. Nebuchadnezzar had required Zedekiah to swear fealty and constant obedience by the true God, whom he called upon to be a witness against him should he break his word; and so, Wesley says, his rebellion was aggravated with perjury and with a horrid contempt of God. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the same threads: all nations, he observes, looked upon an oath as a sacred thing, and on those who durst break through its obligations as the worst of men; though Nebuchadnezzar was a heathen and an enemy, having sworn to him Zedekiah was bound, and to falsify that oath was to learn there is a God to whom vengeance belongs, as Ezek. 17:18 warns. The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as the completing of Zedekiah's self-destruction: a king who would not humble himself before the prophet now perjures himself before the nations, and stiffens against the only turning that could have saved him, until his refusal to return to the LORD leaves nothing between the city and the sword.
14:
The indictment now widens from the throne to the priesthood and the people, and the witnesses read the pollution of the temple as the sin that filled the nation's cup. The reformed John Gill fastens on the special guilt of the leaders: the chief of the priests, who should have instructed the people in the duties of religion and held them to the pure worship of God, were themselves the ringleaders of idolatry, drawing the nation into all the abominations of the heathen round about; and every rank and degree of the people was corrupted with them, as it had been in several of the preceding reigns and was now, a little before the destruction, at its worst.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott refines the terms. “The chiefs” are the princes; “transgressed very much” he renders “committed manifold unfaithfulness”; and the abominations he ties to the vision of Ezek. 8:5-18, where the idolatries within the temple itself are laid bare and the princes of the priests and the people are singled out, the twenty-five men of that vision being, he suggests, the high priest and the heads of the twenty-four courses. He compares too the sweeping charge of Jer. 32:32. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the reading — all the princes of the priests and the people increased faithless transgressions like all the abominations of the heathen, and defiled the house of the LORD which he had hallowed in Jerusalem — while noting the caution of Bertheau (as reported by Keil), who would refer the censure rather to the guilt of the whole people, especially in Manasseh's day, since the book of Jeremiah does not specially fasten idolatry upon the priests and princes of this last hour.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry drives the point home with a proverb of judgment. The priests, the chief of the priests, who should have opposed idolatry, were ringleaders in it; and that place, he warns, is not far from ruin in which religion is already ruined. When the very guardians of the sanctuary lead the way into the abominations of the nations, the defenses of a people are already breached from within. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the defiling of the temple by those consecrated to serve it is the culminating provocation, the sin against the holiest place committed by the holiest office; and that a nation whose priests corrupt its worship has removed the last barrier between itself and the wrath that the next verses will describe as gathering beyond remedy.
15:
Against the swelling guilt the verse sets the long patience of God, and the witnesses linger over the tenderness in the phrase “rising up betimes and sending.” The reformed John Gill names the messengers as the prophets, sent to admonish the people of their idolatries and to warn them of the wrath that would come unless they repented — raised up from the very beginning of the apostasy and continued successively to this hour: Ahijah and Elijah at the first, Amos and Isaiah in the middle, Jeremiah, Zephaniah, and Ezekiel toward the close. The mercy is not a single overture but an unbroken succession of warnings across generations; from the first step the people took toward the idols, Gill notes, God sent to reprove them, so that their whole apostasy was accompanied at every stage by a voice calling them back.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott takes “rising up betimes and sending” to mean constantly and earnestly, and hears in it the very cadence of Jeremiah, who has the LORD sending “all his servants the prophets, rising early and sending them,” at Jer. 25:3-4 and again at Jer. 26:5. The clause “because he had compassion” he renders “he spared, was forbearing with”; and “his dwelling place” is the word Mâʻôn, the temple as God's habitation, as at Ps. 26:8. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley catches the domestic image: God sent his prophets early and diligently, as a careful householder rises betimes to set his servants about their business, giving the people many prophets and many messages, some at the very beginning of their apostasy and others afterward, down to the very day of their captivity.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the verse within the rhetorical build of the passage, in which the transgressions of king and people rise by stages until, in the verses following, the judgment breaks; God sends his messengers because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place, and would by this means have turned away their ruin. The witnesses do not divide. They read the sending of the prophets not as a formality but as the outstretched hand of a God unwilling that any should perish — a patience that reaches back to the first steps of the nation's straying and forward to its last, so that the coming wrath, when it falls, will fall on a people who were warned early, warned often, and warned to the end. The very tenderness of the sending is what will make the mockery of the messengers, in the next verse, so terrible.
16:
The people's answer to God's patience — mockery, contempt, and abuse of his prophets — is read by the witnesses as the sin that at last passed the point of remedy. The reformed John Gill notes plainly that this was the very treatment Jeremiah and Ezekiel so often met with; the messengers of God were mocked, his words despised, his prophets misused, and the record of Jeremiah's own sufferings is the living instance of it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses into the Hebrew, marking that “mocked” is a rare word, an Aramaism occurring only here, and “misused” another word found only here, meaning strictly to stammer or deride. He gathers the fact from the prophets themselves — the scoffing at the word described at Isa. 28:9-14, the idle listeners of Ezek. 33:30, the taunts flung at Jeremiah in Jer. 20:7-8.

Ellicott weighs each of the closing phrases. “Till there was no remedy” is literally “till there was no healing” — no deliverance, no averting of the calamity — for God is said to heal when he turns aside disaster; and “the wrath of the LORD arose” is “went up,” like smoke, the image of Ps. 18:8. The mockery, in other words, did not merely offend; it closed the one door left open, for it was a sin against the very remedy God had provided.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the theology out to its edge. To mock the messengers was a high affront to the God who sent them; to despise his word in their mouths and to misuse the prophets as enemies was an evidence of implacable enmity to God and an invincible resolution to go on in sin. This, Henry says, brought wrath upon them without remedy, for it was sinning against the remedy; nothing is more provoking to God than abuse offered to his faithful ministers, for what is done against them he takes as done against himself — “Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?” He recalls that persecution of God's messengers was the very sin that brought Jerusalem's final destruction by the Romans, as Matt. 23:34-37 foretold. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the turning point of the whole tragedy lies here: not merely in idolatry, but in the scorn of the prophets who called them from it, so that the people themselves shut up the way of escape and left the wrath of God nothing to do but arise.
17:
The wrath that had risen like smoke now descends in the person of the Chaldean king, and the witnesses read the slaughter in the sanctuary as judgment answering to the very place of the sin. The reformed John Gill identifies the instrument as Nebuchadnezzar, and is careful about the divine hand behind it: though it was Zedekiah's rebellion that gave the occasion of his coming, it was the LORD who brought him and gave him success. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears the deliberate echo in the words — “he brought up” the king of the Chaldeans answers to the wrath that “went up” — and observes that the young men were slain “in the house of their sanctuary,” the very temple they had polluted, so that the scene of their sin became the scene of their destruction. The killing without pity of young man and maiden, old man and the gray-headed, he sets beside Ezek. 9, where the horrors of the capture are ascribed expressly to the divine working, and Jer. 15:1-9 and Deut. 32:25.

Ellicott adds a fine grammatical touch: the phrase “he gave them all into his hand” uses a word for “the whole, everything,” not the ordinary word for “all of them,” so that the totality of the surrender is underscored; and he dates the fall of Jerusalem to 588 B.C. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out the somber providence in the name “Chaldees.” Abraham had been called out of Ur of the Chaldees when God took him into covenant, and now his degenerate seed are carried back into that same country, to signify that they had forfeited all the kindness with which they had been loved for their father's sake, and the benefit of the covenant into which he was called.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry completes the picture with an eye to the false refuge the temple had become. Multitudes were put to the sword even in the house of their sanctuary, whither they fled for shelter, hoping the holiness of the place would protect them; but how could they expect that, when they themselves had polluted it with their abominations? Those who cast off the dominion of their religion forfeit all its comfort. The Chaldeans, Henry adds, paid no reverence to the sanctuary and showed no natural pity to the tender or the aged; and justly so, for the people had forsaken the God who had compassion on them, and would have none of him. The witnesses do not divide. They read the massacre as a judgment exactly fitted to the crime — a defiled temple made a slaughterhouse, a scorned mercy turned to unpitying wrath — the fearful working out of the sentence the mocking of the prophets had made inevitable.
18:
The stripping of the temple and the treasuries completes the plunder that the earlier deportations had begun, and the witnesses read the inventory as the total emptying of what had been the richest house on earth. The reformed John Gill marks that these were all the vessels that were left, great and small, for some had already been carried away in the two preceding reigns; now nothing remained to be taken. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch gather the full extent of the seizure: all the vessels of the house of God, the treasures of the temple, and the treasures of the king and of his princes — all of it Nebuchadnezzar brought to Babylon, sacred and secular wealth alike swept away in one act.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott directs the reader to the detailed inventory of the temple furniture at 2 Kings 25:13-17, and to the prophetic notice of the same vessels at Jer. 27:19 and following, where Jeremiah had foretold that even the great pillars and the sea should go to Babylon. The phrase “great and small” he takes as a merism for the whole — from the massive bronze furniture down to the least of the golden implements, not one was spared.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse within the sweep of the desolation: all the remaining vessels of the temple, great and small, and all the treasures, the treasures of God's house and of the king and his princes, were seized and brought to Babylon. He had already drawn the moral that governs the whole plunder — that the people who had brought the idols of the heathen into God's temple were justly punished by having the vessels of that temple carried off to the service of the gods of the nations. The witnesses do not divide. They see in the emptying of the treasuries both a plain fact of conquest and a closing of accounts: the wealth that had been consecrated to the LORD and then profaned by idolatry is now wholly removed from the land, so that the house which the people would not honor with pure worship is left bare, waiting only for the fire that the next verse will bring. The vessels carried off are the visible measure of a glory departed, and their long captivity in Babylon becomes the pledge, as the chapter will show, that a remnant and a return are still to come.
19:
The burning of the temple and the razing of the city bring the judgment to its dreadful climax, and the witnesses record the destruction almost in the cadence of a lament. The reformed John Gill notes simply that they burnt the house of the LORD — the temple itself given to the flames. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch enumerate the ruin: they burnt the house of God, pulled down the walls of Jerusalem, burnt all the palaces of the city with fire, and devoted all its costly vessels to destruction, a verb of “laying waste” they compare with its use at 2 Chron. 12:12.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke measures the loss item by item with a mourner's precision. Here was an end to the temple, the most superb and costly edifice ever erected by man; the wall was broken down, so that Jerusalem ceased to be a fortified city; the palaces were burnt, so that it was no longer a dwelling-place for kings or great men; and the goodly vessels were destroyed, the silver and gold beaten up into shapeless masses, only a few of the finest kept whole. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the details from the parallels — the burning of the house at 2 Kings 25:9, the breaking down of the wall at Jer. 39:8 — and renders the last clause “all her delightsome vessels were for destroying,” echoing the cry of Isa. 64:11, “all our pleasant things are laid waste.” The great vessels, he notes with Kings, were broken up so that their metal might be carried off more easily.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the scene into a single sober warning. The temple was burnt, the walls of Jerusalem demolished, the houses — called palaces for their stateliness — laid in ashes, and all their goodly furniture destroyed; let us see, he says, what woeful havoc sin makes, and, as we value the comfort and continuance of our earthly estates, let us keep that worm from the root of them. The witnesses do not divide. They read the conflagration as the visible end of a long refusal: the house God had chosen for his name, defiled by its worshippers and stripped of its treasures, is now consumed, and the city that had mocked his prophets is left a heap of ashes — yet even here, in the very completeness of the ruin, the reader is being prepared to hear that the desolation has a term, and that the God who sends the fire keeps also the word of restoration.
20:
The carrying away of the survivors into a long Babylonian servitude turns the witnesses to both the fact of the exile and the prophetic word it fulfilled. The reformed John Gill notes that those who had escaped the sword were carried captive, excepting some of the poorer sort left behind to till the land. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the sense precisely: he who remained from the sword — who had not fallen or died in the war — Nebuchadnezzar carried away to Babylon, so that they became servants to him and to his sons until the rise of the kingdom of the Persians, exactly as Jeremiah had prophesied at Jer. 27:7 that all nations should serve him, and his son, and his son's son, until the time of his own land should come.

Keil and Delitzsch read the whole verse, indeed, as the historian's interpretation of prophecy: all this was done that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, who had foretold at Jer. 25:11 and Jer. 29:10 the seventy years' desolation and the Babylonian captivity, while king and people had refused to regard his words. The servitude, then, is not a mere political fact but the visible discharge of a sentence long announced and long despised.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the misery and its strange fruit. The remnant that escaped the sword were carried captive to Babylon, impoverished, enslaved, insulted, and exposed to all the miseries not only of a strange and barbarous land but of an enemy's land, where those who hated them bore rule over them; there they sat down by the rivers of Babylon and mingled their tears with the streams, as Ps. 137:1 remembers. Yet Henry marks a mercy hidden in the chastening: though there they were, it seems, cured of idolatry, they were not, as the prophet Ezekiel shows, cured of mocking the prophets. The witnesses do not divide. They read the exile as judgment and as fulfillment at once — the exact accomplishment of Jeremiah's word to the very people who had scorned it — and yet as a servitude with a stated term, “until the reign of the kingdom of Persia,” so that the sentence carries within it the promise of its own ending, and the captives by the rivers of Babylon are not cast off forever but corrected for a season.
21:
The land's long rest “until she had enjoyed her sabbaths” gathers the witnesses around the deep justice of the seventy years, in which an abused land recovers by force what its people had defrauded it of by neglect. The reformed John Gill reads it plainly: the Jews were so long servants in Babylon in order to accomplish Jeremiah's prophecy of the seventy years. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch see the Chronicler pointing out how exactly God had fulfilled his word by the mouth of the prophet, the desolation of the land running its appointed course to the very number Jeremiah had named.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott unfolds the language and the arithmetic. The seventy years of exile are predicted at Jer. 25:11-12 and Jer. 29:10; the word rendered “enjoyed” Gesenius takes to mean “made good” or “discharged,” as a debt is paid, so that through the long years of the captivity the land at last received the rest of which it had been defrauded by the neglect of the sabbatical years commanded at Lev. 25:1-7. The clause “as long as she lay desolate she kept sabbath” he shows to be drawn from Lev. 26:34-35. But he warns against pressing the words too far: we have no right to assume the sacred writer means that exactly seventy sabbatical years had been neglected, which would require the law to have gone unobserved for four hundred and ninety years; the seventy, he reckons, are counted from the fourth year of Jehoiakim, when the prophecy was uttered, to the first of Cyrus and the return under Zerubbabel in 536 B.C.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds in the desolation both a punishment and a strange pledge. As God had threatened by Moses at Lev. 26:34, the land now enjoyed the rest it had been denied; the people had many a time plowed and sowed in the seventh year when the ground should have rested, and now it lay unplowed and unsown for ten times seven years. God will be no loser in his glory by the disobedience of men: if they would not let the land rest, God would make it rest whether they would or no. Yet Henry hears an encouragement in it too — had others come and taken possession, the exiles might have despaired of recovery, but while the land lay desolate it seemed, as it were, to lie waiting for them, refusing to acknowledge any other owners. The witnesses do not divide. They read the sabbath-keeping of the emptied land as the exact and even the arithmetical justice of God, and as the quiet assurance that a people corrected for a set term were meant, at its close, to come home.
22:
With the edict of Cyrus the book turns from judgment to hope, and the witnesses first weigh whether these closing verses belong to the Chronicle at all. The reformed John Gill observes that the two verses are the same with which the book of Ezra opens, and that this overlap is a strong presumption that one and the same person, Ezra, wrote both books; or else, he allows, a transcriber who had finished the Chronicles at the twenty-first verse went on into Ezra without a stop, and, perceiving his mistake, broke off abruptly — which would explain why the sentence here ends in mid-air. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes the latter view more decidedly: this verse and the next are supposed to have been written by mistake from the book of Ezra, the Chronicles properly closing with the twenty-first verse at the onset of the captivity, whereas these speak of events seventy years later, in the first year of Cyrus over the empire of the East.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, by contrast, treat the passage as the Chronicler's own deliberate close, added to point out still further how exactly God had fulfilled his word by the mouth of Jeremiah: in the first year of Cyrus the LORD stirred up the spirit of the Persian king to send a proclamation through all his kingdom, that Jahve the God of heaven, who had given him all the kingdoms of the earth, had charged him to build a house at Jerusalem, and that whoever belonged to the people of God might go up. With this comforting prospect for the future, they note, the author of the Chronicle closes his work.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds the philological detail. The verse is nearly identical with Ezra 1:1; “stirred up the spirit” is the idiom of 1 Chron. 5:26; “made a proclamation” is literally “made a voice pass,” as at 2 Chron. 30:5; and the “writing” is the term used at 2 Chron. 35:4. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the theology: these verses look back to Jeremiah's prophecy and show it accomplished, for God had promised the restoring of the captives and the rebuilding of Jerusalem at the end of seventy years, and that set time to favor Zion came at last; after a long and dark night the day-spring from on high visited them, and God was found true to every word he had spoken. The witnesses divide only over the seam — whether original close or borrowed opening — but agree in substance: the same seventy years whose neglect had emptied the land are now fulfilled unto mercy, and the God who stirred up the Chaldean to destroy now stirs up the Persian to restore.
23:
The proclamation of Cyrus stands as the book's last word, and the witnesses read it as at once the fulfillment of prophecy and a marvel of divine sovereignty over a pagan king. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the substance of the decree: Cyrus confesses that the LORD God of heaven has given him all the kingdoms of the earth and has charged him to build him a house in Jerusalem, and he sends up whoever among God's people will go, with the blessing “The LORD his God be with him.” Here, they observe, the Chronicle deliberately ends — not on the ashes of the temple but on the open door of return, a comforting prospect set as the final note of the whole history.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the broken syntax and the strange piety of the words. The sentence “and let him go up” halts abruptly — “go up whither?” — the clause being completed only in Ezra 1:3. The royal formula “Thus saith Cyrus, king of Persia” he compares with the openings of Darius on the Behistun Inscription, “I am Darius, the great king, the king of kings”; and the claim that all the kingdoms have been “given me” he sets beside Darius's own “by the grace of Ormazd I am king.” The title “the God of heaven,” he notes, was itself a name of Ormazd, the supreme being of Persian belief; it is not at all wonderful, then, that Cyrus should identify the God of Israel with his own deity, especially if he had heard the prophecies of Isa. 44:28 that named him — a politic syncretism such as later ages would see again in the practice of Rome.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke closes the book with a backward gaze over the whole. The Targum, he notes, paraphrases the blessing as “Let the Word of the LORD be his helper, and let him go up.” And so ends, Clarke reflects, the history of a people the most fickle, the most ungrateful, and perhaps on the whole the most sinful that ever existed on the face of the earth — yet what a display it gives of the power, justice, mercy, and long-suffering of the LORD; there was no people like this people, and no God like their God. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had drawn the same consolation: though God's church be cast down, it is not cast off; though thrown into the furnace, his people are not left there longer than till the dross be separated, and the Israel of God shall be fetched out of Babylon in due time, and even the dry bones made to live. The witnesses do not divide. They read the last verse as a door left open at the end of a chronicle of ruin — a heathen emperor moved by the God of heaven to send a captive people home, so that the book of Judah's fall ends not in Babylon but on the road up to Jerusalem.
